name: Scleral cosmetic lenses

image.caption: Dry eyes scleral lens on removal plunger

lead: Scleral lenses are large rigid gas-permeable contact lenses that vault over the cornea and rest on the sclera, the white of the eye, with a tear-filled space beneath [1]. Versions without fluid reservoirs are used as film and costume effects to give characters unusual eye colours [1].

Their medical role is large: they are used for conditions such as keratoconus, severe dry eye, and ocular surface disease, where they can improve comfort and vision [1][2][3]. Where a lens is tinted or painted, it can also alter how the eye looks.

paras: Lenses are custom fitted by eye-care specialists, often with trial sets or imaging, and are cleaned between uses; they are not worn during sleep [1][4].
Reviews describe complications and fitting challenges; studies have measured corneal oedema, oxygen transmission and intraocular pressure effects with wear [4][5][6].

angle.text: Tinted or painted scleral lenses change or mask how the eye looks, and medical versions smooth vision over an irregular cornea.

lead: Scleral lenses are large-diameter lenses that rest on the sclera and vault over the cornea, leaving a fluid layer; modern ones use highly oxygen-permeable material [1]. Designs date from the 1880s, passing through blown glass, ground glass and PMMA before returning in the 1970s with gas-permeable materials [1].

For appearance, versions without a fluid reservoir are common in film and television, and in costume design to show unusually coloured eyes [1]. Medical scleral lenses also serve as protective, prosthetic-style devices, for example in graft-versus-host disease dry eye [2].
A substantial clinical literature covers keratoconus, dry eye and complications [3][4][5][6][7].

paras: The lens clears the cornea and bears on the conjunctiva over the sclera, creating a tear reservoir [1]. Fitting aims for corneal clearance and scleral alignment, sometimes using imaging [8].

Randomised trials examined tear dynamics under lenses [9], intraocular pressure by lens size and wear time [10] and oxygen diffusion and corneal oedema [6]. A trial in keratoconus reported improved vision-related quality of life with mini-scleral lenses [7], and a meta-analysis reviewed keratoconus outcomes [11]. A case series of 33 patients with chronic graft-versus-host disease examined symptoms and quality of life with a scleral prosthetic device [2]. These studies address medical use rather than cosmetic outcomes.
A review describes complications and fitting challenges of scleral lenses [4].
